section.title: David Anointed
section.sectionRationale: Chapter 15 ended with Samuel grieving over Saul's rejection as king. Chapter 16 opens with the LORD moving Samuel past that grief to Bethlehem, where He passes over Jesse's impressive older sons and chooses the youngest, a shepherd boy, because the LORD looks on the heart rather than the appearance. Samuel anoints David quietly among his brothers, and the Spirit of the LORD rushes upon him from that day forward, even as the Spirit departs from Saul, who is now troubled by a spirit of distress. Through David's skill with the harp, the newly anointed but still hidden king enters Saul's own household as a musician and armor bearer, quietly gaining a place at court long before Israel knows who he really is.
section.thesis: While Samuel and Israel are drawn to height and appearance, the LORD chooses and anoints the youngest, least likely son because He looks on the heart, and by His providence quietly places this hidden king in Saul's own household to be shaped for the throne he does not yet openly hold.
section.frameNote: Four beats: Samuel sent in secret to Bethlehem, verses 1 to 5; the brothers passed over because the LORD sees the heart, verses 6 to 10; the anointing of David and the Spirit rushing upon him, verses 11 to 13; and David's quiet entrance into Saul's service as the Spirit departs from Saul, verses 14 to 23.

verses.text: Now the LORD said to Samuel, “How long are you going to mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him as king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil and go. I am sending you to Jesse of Bethlehem, for I have selected from his sons a king for Myself.”
“How can I go?” Samuel asked. “Saul will hear of it and kill me!” The LORD answered, “Take a heifer with you and say, ‘I have come to sacrifice to the LORD.’
Then invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what you are to do. You are to anoint for Me the one I indicate.”
So Samuel did what the LORD had said and went to Bethlehem. When the elders of the town met him, they trembled and asked, “Do you come in peace?”
“In peace,” he replied. “I have come to sacrifice to the LORD. Consecrate yourselves and come with me to the sacrifice.” Then he consecrated Jesse and his sons and invited them to the sacrifice.

units.label: Not as man sees
units.note: the LORD looks on the heart

verses.text: When they arrived, Samuel saw Eliab and said, “Surely here before the LORD is His {{mashiach|anointed}}.”

But the LORD said to Samuel, “Do not consider his appearance or height, for I have rejected him; the LORD does not see as man does. For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the {{lebab|heart}}.”
Then Jesse called Abinadab and presented him to Samuel, who said, “The LORD has not chosen this one either.”
Next Jesse presented Shammah, but Samuel said, “The LORD has not chosen this one either.”
Thus Jesse made seven of his sons pass before Samuel, but Samuel told him, “The LORD has not chosen any of these.”

And Samuel asked him, “Are these all the sons you have?” “There is still the youngest,” Jesse replied, “but he is tending the sheep.” “Send for him,” Samuel replied. “For we will not sit down to eat until he arrives.”
So Jesse sent for his youngest son and brought him in. He was ruddy, with beautiful eyes and a handsome appearance. And the LORD said, “Rise and anoint him, for he is the one.”
So Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the presence of his brothers, and the {{ruach|Spirit}} of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward. Then Samuel set out and went to Ramah.
Now the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul, and a spirit of distress from the LORD began to torment him.
Saul’s servants said to him, “Surely a spirit of distress from God is tormenting you.
Let our lord command your servants here to seek out someone who can skillfully play the harp. Whenever the spirit of distress from God is upon you, he is to play it, and you will be well.”
And Saul commanded his servants, “Find me someone who plays well, and bring him to me.”
One of the servants answered, “I have seen a son of Jesse of Bethlehem who knows how to play the harp. He is a mighty man of valor, a warrior, eloquent and handsome, and the LORD is with him.”
So Saul sent messengers to Jesse and said, “Send me your son David, who is with the sheep.”
And Jesse took a donkey loaded with bread, a skin of wine, and one young goat and sent them to Saul with his son David.
When David came to Saul and entered his service, Saul loved him very much, and David became his armor-bearer.
Then Saul sent word to Jesse, saying, “Let David remain in my service, for I am pleased with him.”
And whenever the spirit from God came upon Saul, David would pick up his harp and play. Then Saul would find relief and feel better, and the spirit of distress would depart from him.

mashiach.gloss: Anointed one, someone set apart to an office, especially king or priest, by the pouring of oil. Samuel first guesses Eliab is the LORD's mashiach by his looks alone; the true mashiach, David, is the youngest and least expected. The title points forward to ha-mashiach, the Anointed One, Jesus Christ, the true and final Anointed King and Priest.

lebab.gloss: Heart, the inner person, mind, will, and settled character, not merely emotion. Where man sees the outward appearance, the LORD sees the lebab, so David is chosen for who he is within rather than his stature or looks.

ruach.gloss: Spirit, wind, breath. The ruach of the LORD rushes upon David the moment he is anointed, empowering him for the calling God has appointed, in the same chapter that the ruach departs from Saul, marking a decisive transfer of God's enabling presence from the rejected king to the chosen one.

basic.context: Chapter 15 left Samuel grieving over Saul, whom the LORD had rejected as king. Chapter 16 opens with God moving Samuel past that grief into action, sending him to Bethlehem to anoint a successor from among Jesse's sons. Samuel expects the tall, impressive Eliab to be the one, but the LORD stops him: He does not choose the way people do. One by one, seven sons pass before Samuel, and none is chosen, until Jesse's youngest, forgotten out with the sheep, is sent for and anointed. From that day the Spirit of the LORD rushes upon David, even as it departs from Saul, who begins to be tormented by a spirit of distress. Through a court servant's recommendation, David, already anointed but not yet enthroned, quietly enters Saul's household as a musician whose playing soothes the troubled king. The key questions the chapter raises are why God passes over the obvious choices, what it means that the LORD looks at the heart, and why the anointed king remains hidden in humble service rather than immediately taking the throne.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative describing a real, one time anointing, not a formula guaranteeing that the youngest or least impressive person is always God's choice. What the chapter does teach as an enduring truth is how God evaluates people, by the heart rather than appearance or rank. The chapter also raises a fair question about the spirit of distress said to come from the LORD upon Saul, verse 14, which needs careful handling so that God's sovereignty over all things, even judgment, is affirmed without making Him the author of evil.
basic.originalLanguages: Samuel almost anoints Eliab as the mashiach, the anointed one, based on appearance, but the LORD corrects him: people judge by what they can see, while the LORD examines the lebab, the heart. When David is finally anointed, the ruach, the Spirit of the LORD, rushes upon him from that day forward, the very moment the same Spirit departs from Saul, marking whose reign God is now building toward.
basic.typology: David is anointed king yet continues in quiet, hidden service, tending sheep and later serving in Saul's court, long before he visibly reigns. This pattern of an anointed one who is truly king yet lives for a time in humility and service before being openly enthroned points forward to Jesus, the true Anointed King who lived in humble obscurity and servanthood before His enthronement was made plain to the world.
basic.christ: David is chosen not for outward stature but because the LORD looks on the heart, and the Spirit rushes upon him at his anointing, equipping him for a reign that has not yet begun. In the same way, Jesus is God's true Anointed One, esteemed by the world as having no stately form or majesty, Isaiah 53:2, yet anointed with the Spirit without limit at His baptism, Luke 3:22, and truly King from the very moment of that anointing though His enthronement was not yet openly displayed. Where David waited years in hidden faithfulness before his coronation, Christ endured a season of humble obedience before being exalted to the throne at the Father's right hand.
basic.god: God is free and sovereign in whom He chooses, refusing to be bound by human standards of height, birth order, or appearance, and instead searching the heart. He is also sovereign over Saul's unraveling, a spirit of distress from the LORD troubling the king He has rejected, showing that even affliction and consequence remain under His hand rather than outside it. And He is a God who provides comfort in the midst of judgment, giving Saul relief through David's music even while working out His larger purpose of replacing him.
basic.crossReferences: First Samuel 15 explains why a new king is needed after Saul's disobedience. Psalm 78 later celebrates that God took David from tending the ewes to shepherd Jacob, His people. Paul's sermon in Acts 13 cites God's testimony that David was a man after His own heart. And Paul tells the Corinthians that God chose what is lowly and despised in the world, the same pattern seen in the choosing of the youngest son.
basic.oneStory: Israel asked for a king like the nations and received Saul, who is now rejected for his disobedience. Here the LORD begins to raise up a king after His own heart, anointing David while he is still young, unknown, and out with the sheep. The chapter is one more step in the long story of God choosing the humble and unlikely to carry His purposes, a pattern that reaches its fullness in Jesus, the true Anointed King born in humble circumstances and revealed in God's own time.

context.literary:
The chapter is engineered around delay and reversal. Seven sons pass before Samuel, and the narrative slows to name each rejection individually, verses 8 to 10, building an expectation the reader shares with Samuel, surely the next one, only to have it denied again and again. The delay is the point, by the time the youngest is finally sent for, the reader has felt, in miniature, exactly what the LORD's words in verse 7 mean, since every plausible candidate available to human judgment has now been tried and found wanting.

The chapter also folds two scenes together that at first glance seem unrelated, a quiet family sacrifice in Bethlehem and a court crisis in Gibeah, joined by nothing but a single conjunction, now, verse 14. The seam is deliberate. David's anointing, told in three verses, and his years of hidden preparation are compressed almost to nothing, while the description of his skill and character, verse 18, is given at unusual length for a court servant's recommendation, functioning almost as a second, human confirmation of what the LORD had just told Samuel in secret.

The unit closes on an image that will recur throughout David's story, music offered to calm a troubled king, planting, this early, the instrument that later carries so many of David's own psalms, and quietly establishing David inside Saul's household long before Israel, or Saul himself, understands what has actually just happened.
context.historical:
Samuel's fear in verse 2, that Saul will kill him if the anointing becomes known, is not paranoia, anointing a rival king while the reigning king still lives was, in the plainest political terms, an act of treason, and Saul had already shown at Gilgal how quickly fear could turn to violence. The sacrifice at Bethlehem gives Samuel legitimate cover, since a small town's elders would expect a travelling prophet or priest to arrive for exactly this kind of local worship, and their trembling question, do you come in peace, verse 4, shows how unusual and potentially dangerous any unannounced visit from Samuel could seem even to ordinary townspeople.

The horn of oil in verse 1 marks a different kind of anointing than Saul received. Saul was anointed from a flask, 1 Samuel 10:1, the same kind of vessel later used for Jehu, a king whose dynasty would not endure past a few generations, 2 Kings 9:1-3, David, like Solomon after him, is anointed from a horn, 1 Kings 1:39, the vessel associated with an enduring line.

Court musicians who could calm a troubled ruler were a recognized feature of ancient Near Eastern royal households, and informal service as an armor bearer, alongside such musical duty, was an ordinary way for a capable young man without noble rank to gain standing and proximity to the king, exactly the door through which David enters Saul's own court.
context.canonical:
This chapter answers a question the book has been asking since chapter 8, what will Israel's king actually be measured by. Saul had been chosen partly because he stood a head taller than anyone else, 1 Samuel 9:2, and even called himself the least likely candidate from the smallest clan of the smallest tribe, 1 Samuel 9:21, a humility that did not survive his rise. David is chosen from an even more overlooked position, a shepherd boy not even brought in for the first round of introductions, and the LORD explicitly names the standard that will define every king from here on, appearance against heart, verse 7.

That standard becomes a refrain. David himself will later ask God to search him and know his heart, Psalm 139:23, and instruct Solomon to serve the LORD with a whole heart, since the LORD searches every heart and understands every intent, 1 Chronicles 28:9. Centuries later Jeremiah will call the heart deceitful above all things and declare that the LORD alone searches it, Jeremiah 17:9-10, and Jesus will tell His accusers to stop judging by outward appearance and start judging justly, John 7:24.

The chapter also quietly begins the story of a hidden king serving in plain sight, David the anointed shepherd become armor bearer, that will not fully resolve until 2 Samuel 5, when all Israel finally makes him king in public what God had already made him in private in this one small Bethlehem sacrifice.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: By slowing down for each of Jesse's seven older sons and letting Samuel's own expectation be corrected verse by verse, the author wants his hearers to feel, not just be told, how differently God evaluates a candidate than even a trusted prophet does. Samuel is not a fool here, he is simply human, reading Eliab the way Israel once read Saul, and the narrative uses that very human misjudgment to drive home its point more forcefully than a bare statement could. The writer also means the placement of this chapter, immediately after Saul's final rejection and immediately before David's public rise in chapter 17, to be read as cause and effect, the Spirit's departure from Saul and arrival on David is not incidental timing but the narrative's own explanation for everything that follows in both men's lives, the one increasingly tormented, the other increasingly capable, long before either outcome is visible to the wider nation.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The chapter records a specific historical anointing and a specific instance of an afflicting spirit, it is not a manual for identifying future leaders by looking for the youngest or least likely candidate in the room, nor does it teach that God routinely sends tormenting spirits on everyone who disobeys Him. What does transfer as abiding instruction is the principle stated explicitly in verse 7, that human judgment reliably overvalues what can be seen and undervalues what cannot, and the sobering reality, stated just as plainly in verse 14, that God remains sovereign even over the distressing consequences of a settled, rejected life, so that nothing in Saul's unraveling, however painful, ever slips outside the LORD's own governance.

debates.question: What is the 'spirit of distress from the LORD' that torments Saul, verse 14?

views.label: A judicial affliction God directly sends
views.case: The text plainly says the spirit is from the LORD, and it parallels other passages, such as 1 Kings 22:19-23, where God sovereignly permits a spirit to bring about judgment on a rejected king; this reads Saul's torment as a direct consequence of his own disobedience, sent under God's authority as discipline.

views.label: God's sovereign withdrawal allowing an evil spirit's activity
views.case: Once the Spirit of the LORD departs, verse 14, protection and blessing are withdrawn, and a harmful spirit, as the footnote allows, is free to trouble Saul; God is sovereign over this happening, permitting rather than authoring the evil itself.

debates.bearing: Either reading affirms that Saul's unraveling flows from his own rejection of God's word and that nothing, not even a tormenting spirit, operates outside God's sovereign authority; neither view makes God the author of evil, and both magnify His justice and His sovereign rule.

debates.question: Was Samuel wrong to fear Saul and ask for cover before going to Bethlehem, verses 1 to 2?

views.label: A reasonable precaution, not unbelief
views.case: God Himself supplies the cover story, verses 2 to 3, rather than rebuking Samuel's fear, showing that the LORD accommodates a realistic danger instead of demanding reckless disregard for it; wisdom and courage are not opposites, and God works through Samuel's ordinary caution rather than only through fearless bravado.

views.label: A telling sign that fear still shadowed even a faithful prophet
views.case: Samuel had just spent a full chapter grieving over Saul and needed God's own prompting even to move at all, verse 1; his hesitation here shows that even God's most faithful servants can need direct, repeated instruction to act, a pattern echoed later in Elijah's fear under Jezebel, 1 Kings 19.

debates.bearing: Either way, God does not shame Samuel for asking how, He simply gives him a legitimate way forward, showing that trusting God does not always mean discounting real danger, and that God is willing to work through ordinary caution rather than only through visible boldness.

study.originalLanguages:
Samuel comes to Bethlehem carrying not the flask that anointed Saul, 1 Samuel 10:1, but a horn, verse 1. The distinction is not stylistic. A flask empties and is set aside, a horn, hollow and curved, was itself sometimes used to store oil precisely because it did not spill or crack the way a clay vessel could. The same word, horn, anoints Solomon later, 1 Kings 1:39, while the flask reappears for Jehu, 2 Kings 9:1-3, a king whose own dynasty barely outlasts four generations. The vessel in each anointing quietly forecasts the durability of the reign it inaugurates.

Verse 7 turns on a single repeated Hebrew verb, to see. Man sees for the eyes, but the LORD sees for the heart, is a more literal rendering of what the BSB smooths into appearance and heart, the Hebrew uses the identical verb twice, so that the difference God is naming is not that He perceives while we do not, but that He and we are looking at two entirely different things when we look at the very same man.

The verb behind the Spirit rushed upon David, verse 13, is a root so flexible it also means to succeed or prosper, the same word used of Joseph, the LORD made him prosper in all he did, Genesis 39:3. One Hebrew verb carries both senses at once, a sudden, forceful coming and a lasting fruitfulness, so that David's anointing is described, in its very grammar, as the beginning of a life that will prosper because the Spirit has come upon it. The same verb also describes the Spirit coming powerfully on Samson, Judges 14:6, and rushing on Saul himself at his own anointing, 1 Samuel 10:6, a single word linking three very different men's beginnings.

The affliction that troubles Saul, by contrast, is called harmful, the ordinary Hebrew word behind evil throughout the Old Testament, not softened or hedged the way spirit of distress can sound in English. And David himself is introduced as ruddy, verse 12, the same word used of Esau at his birth, Genesis 25:25, two ruddy men whose stories could hardly run in more opposite directions, one who despised a birthright he already held, the other who receives, quietly and without asking, a kingdom he does not yet hold at all.

typology.type: David anointed yet remaining in hidden, humble service
typology.fulfillment: Between his anointing in verse 13 and his public coronation years later, David serves first as a shepherd, then as a court musician and armor bearer, an anointed king functioning as a servant in someone else's household. Christ's hiddenness runs even longer, thirty quiet years in Nazareth before a single public sign of His kingship, Luke 3:23, and Paul says He did not consider equality with God something to be grasped but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, Philippians 2:6-7. The correspondence holds all the way to its outcome, since both men's hidden service ends in public exaltation, though only Christ's exaltation is to a throne that will never again be threatened.

typology.type: The Spirit rushing upon the anointed one
typology.fulfillment: The Spirit rushes upon David the moment the horn of oil touches him, verse 13, equipping him for a throne he will not visibly hold for years. The same Spirit descends on Jesus at His baptism, this time visibly, like a dove, and remains, John 1:32-33, an anointing the Baptist recognizes as proof that this is the One who will himself baptize with the Holy Spirit. Isaiah had already promised a shoot from Jesse's own stump on whom the Spirit of the LORD would rest, Isaiah 11:1-2, so that this chapter's anointing of Jesse's youngest becomes, centuries later, the very picture Isaiah reaches for to describe great David's greater descendant.

typology.type: The LORD looking on the heart rather than outward appearance
typology.fulfillment: Samuel's near mistake with Eliab becomes the standard every reader is meant to carry forward, since the LORD does not see as man sees. Jesus rebukes the same reflex in His opponents, stop judging by outward appearances and start judging justly, John 7:24, and He alone, unlike any human judge, actually sees every heart without needing correction, searching hearts and minds, Revelation 2:23. Where Samuel had to be stopped and taught to look past Eliab's stature, Christ never needs to unlearn a wrong impression, because nothing about anyone's heart is hidden from Him in the first place.

typology.type: The horn of oil that does not run empty
typology.fulfillment: Saul was anointed from a flask, a vessel with a limit, the same kind used later for Jehu, a king whose own line collapsed within a few generations, 2 Kings 9:1-3. David is anointed from a horn, as Solomon will be after him, 1 Kings 1:39, a vessel that carries, even in its shape, a picture of a dynasty meant to endure. Jesus is given the Spirit without any vessel or measure at all, without limit, John 3:34, so that what a horn could only symbolize, an anointing that does not run out, is finally realized without any symbol left to stand in for it.

study.christ:
Samuel's near mistake with Eliab is worth pausing on, because it is not really about Eliab at all, it is about how easily even a good and godly judge can mistake impressive packaging for divine appointment. Israel's whole history with Saul was itself Exhibit A of that mistake, a king chosen partly for his height, 1 Samuel 9:2, whose story chapter 15 has just finished narrating to its bitter end. God will not let that mistake repeat itself in the choosing of the next king, and the correction He gives Samuel in verse 7 becomes, centuries later, the very principle by which the true King is finally recognized at all, since Isaiah warns in advance that this King will have no stately form or majesty to attract us, no beauty that we should desire Him, Isaiah 53:2, a Messiah whose glory, like David's, would not announce itself through appearance.

David's anointing here is real but incomplete, a private, hidden coronation years ahead of any public reign. Jesus experiences a strikingly similar gap, anointed with the Spirit at His baptism in a very public moment, yet still spending the years immediately after in obscurity before His ministry properly begins, and even then walking toward a throne He will not visibly occupy until after a crucifixion. Where David's hidden years were spent tending sheep and playing music to soothe a troubled king who did not yet know he was entertaining his own successor, Christ's hidden years were spent in a carpenter's shop, and even His public ministry looked, to most who watched it, like anything but the reign of a king.

The link between the two men is not incidental. Isaiah names a shoot that will spring up from the very stump of Jesse whose sons pass one by one before Samuel in this chapter, and says the Spirit of the LORD will rest on Him, wisdom, counsel, and strength, Isaiah 11:1-2. What begins as an anointing hidden even from most of David's own household becomes, in Jesus, an anointing without any limit or measure at all, John 3:34, poured out not on a shepherd boy for a throne still years away, but on the Son of God for a kingdom that has already, in principle, begun.
study.god:
Samuel very nearly canonizes Eliab as God's anointed on sight, before God ever speaks, verse 6, and it takes a direct correction for even Israel's own prophet to unlearn the reflex that judges by stature. What this reveals about God is not simply that He prefers modest people, but that His evaluation runs on an entirely different axis than ours, the Hebrew text repeats the verb see in both halves of God's correction in verse 7, man sees for the eyes, but the LORD sees for the heart, the identical verb applied to two entirely different objects, showing that the difference between human and divine judgment is not less perception but a different object of perception altogether.

He also works through deliberate concealment rather than only through public announcement. Samuel is sent in secret, given a cover story God Himself supplies, verse 2, and told to anoint David quietly among his own brothers rather than before the nation, verse 13. A God who could simply depose Saul and enthrone David by open decree instead chooses a slow, hidden, almost domestic beginning, showing that His timing is not our timing and that a throne can be settled in heaven's counsel years before it is settled in anyone else's sight.

He remains sovereign over what happens to the king He has just replaced, and Scripture does not flinch from saying so plainly, a spirit of distress from the LORD begins to torment Saul the very same day the Spirit rushes upon David, verse 14. This is not two unrelated events, it is one transfer of favor described from both sides at once, and the text's own honesty about attributing Saul's torment to the LORD, rather than pretending it happened outside His governance, is itself a claim about how completely His rule extends, even into consequences that feel to the sufferer like abandonment.

And He is not without mercy even here. The very music that soothes Saul's torment comes from the hand of the man God has already chosen to replace him, so that Saul receives real, ordinary comfort from the very future he is losing, a small and almost startling kindness folded into the middle of his own unraveling.

crossReferences.note: Saul is introduced as choice and handsome, a head taller than anyone in Israel, the very measure by which Israel first wanted a king. This chapter deliberately overturns that measure, choosing a youngest son summoned in from the sheep, so that the contrast between the two anointings is drawn as sharply as the narrator can manage.

The psalm later summarizes this chapter in three lines, God took David from tending the ewes to shepherd His people, guiding them with skillful hands and a heart of integrity. What Samuel witnesses in one afternoon at Bethlehem becomes, generations later, the settled memory of how Israel's greatest king actually began.

David later tells Solomon to serve God wholeheartedly, for the LORD searches every heart and understands every intent. Having been chosen himself by that very standard, David passes on to his son the same truth Samuel had to learn on the spot in Bethlehem, that appearances before God count for nothing next to the heart's true direction.

The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure, Jeremiah says, and only the LORD can search it and know it truly. The verse explains why God's method in this chapter is not one Samuel, or anyone else, could ever have managed on his own, since the very organ being judged is too devious for human courts to read.

Paul reminds a proud church that not many of them were wise, powerful, or highborn when God called them, because He chooses what is weak and despised precisely so no one can boast in His presence. David's own unlikely calling from the sheepfolds is one Old Testament instance of the very pattern Paul describes centuries later.

Paul later tells a synagogue in Pisidian Antioch that God removed Saul and raised up David, testifying of him, I have found David a man after My own heart, who will do all My will. Luke lets the crowd hear, in a single breath, the verdict this chapter only shows unfolding slowly, one rejected son at a time.

Centuries later a different king, Ahab, is enticed to his death by a spirit the LORD allows into the mouths of his prophets, a scene that helps frame how Saul's spirit of distress can genuinely come from the LORD without making Him the author of the evil it produces.

God gives the Spirit without limit to the One He sends, John says of Jesus. David receives the Spirit at his anointing in this chapter for a specific calling that will still take years to unfold, the Son receives it without any measure or limit at all, the difference between an anointed shepherd boy and the Anointed One Himself.

Solomon, like David before him, is anointed from a horn of oil rather than the flask used for Saul, and the whole city erupts in a joy so loud the earth itself seems to split. The horn becomes, across three anointings, a quiet sign of the enduring line God is building through David's house.

study.oneStory:
Long before Bethlehem, the LORD had already shown that He weighs what people cannot see. Just before the flood He looked not at humanity's achievements but at the intent of every heart and found it corrupted through and through, Genesis 6:5, centuries later He looks at seven strong sons in one small town and finds, instead, a shepherd boy their own father had not thought to call in from the fields. The method is the same even when the verdict runs in the opposite direction, a God who searches hearts, for judgment in Noah's day and for calling in David's.

This chapter marks the moment the promised king after God's own heart, announced but not yet named back in chapter 13, finally receives a name and a face. Everything that follows in David's long, uneven life, his courage before Goliath, his years fleeing Saul, his own great sins and his greater repentance, grows out of this one afternoon in Bethlehem, where a horn of oil and a rushing Spirit mark him out years before anyone else can see it.

The chapter does not resolve the tension it creates. David is anointed yet unenthroned, chosen yet still tending sheep and later playing harp in another man's court, a hidden king serving in someone else's house. That tension will not fully resolve in David's own lifetime, and it will not fully resolve even in his dynasty, since David's own sons will fail the very heart-standard set here. It resolves only in great David's greater Son, anointed with the Spirit without limit, John 3:34, who also lived for thirty hidden years in a carpenter's house before His kingship was ever publicly declared, and who is finally seen, at the very end of the story, worthy to take the scroll because He was slain, gathering a kingdom and priests to reign forever, Revelation 5:9-10, the search that began in a shepherd's field in Bethlehem ending at a throne no one will ever tear away again.

quiz.q: Why does the LORD reject Eliab even though Samuel is sure he is the one?

options.text: The LORD does not see as man sees; man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart, v7.
options.note: This is the LORD's own explicit reason to Samuel in verse 7.

options.text: Samuel judged by outward stature, just as Israel once judged Saul, but God's standard for this king is different.
options.note: True and related, but it is a broader observation rather than the text's stated reason.

options.text: Eliab was too old and had already missed his opportunity to be chosen.
options.note: Age or birth order is not given as the reason; the stated reason is the heart, not appearance.

options.text: There was no reason given; the choice was arbitrary.
options.note: The LORD gives a clear reason, seeing the heart rather than appearance, so it is not arbitrary.

quiz.q: What happens the moment David is anointed, and what happens to Saul in the same chapter?

options.text: The Spirit of the LORD rushes upon David from that day forward, even as the Spirit departs from Saul, marking a transfer of God's empowering presence.
options.note: Verses 13-14 place these two events side by side deliberately.

options.text: David becomes instantly popular with all the people of Israel.
options.note: David's reputation does grow later in the chapter, but the immediate, stated result of the anointing is the Spirit rushing upon him.

options.text: David receives the Spirit only because he could already play the harp well.
options.note: His musical skill is mentioned afterward, but it is not the reason the Spirit comes upon him at his anointing.

options.text: Nothing changes for David; he simply returns to tending the sheep with no further mention of the Spirit.
options.note: The text explicitly says the Spirit rushed upon him from that day forward.

quiz.q: What does the spirit of distress that torments Saul reveal, verses 14-16?

options.text: It shows that even Saul's affliction after his rejection remains under the LORD's sovereign hand, not outside it.
options.note: The text names it a spirit of distress from the LORD, keeping God's sovereignty central even here.

options.text: It shows an evil power operating completely apart from any relationship to God's rule.
options.note: There is real trouble here, but the text ties its origin to the LORD's sovereign action or permission, not to a power independent of Him.

options.text: It shows that Saul was simply experiencing ordinary sadness unrelated to his rejection as king.
options.note: The narrative directly connects the affliction to the Spirit's departure after his rejection, not mere ordinary sadness.

options.text: It shows that David's music had no real effect on Saul at all.
options.note: Verse 23 says Saul found relief and felt better when David played.

quiz.q: Why was David initially left out when Jesse presented his sons to Samuel?

options.text: David, the youngest, was overlooked and left tending sheep until Samuel insisted every son be brought before him.
options.note: Verse 11 shows Jesse did not even think to include his youngest son at first.

options.text: Jesse deliberately hid David to protect him from being noticed by Saul.
options.note: The text gives no such motive; David was simply out with the sheep as the youngest son.

options.text: David refused to come because he did not want to be anointed.
options.note: David is sent for and comes; there is no refusal on his part in the text.

options.text: David was actually the firstborn and always expected to be chosen.
options.note: David is explicitly the youngest of the sons, the least expected choice.

quiz.q: What is significant about David entering Saul's service as a musician and armor bearer?

options.text: God's providence quietly placed the newly anointed but still hidden king in Saul's own household, gaining him experience and access to the court before Israel knew who he was.
options.note: The chapter shows David's anointing followed immediately by an unlikely, provident door into Saul's court.

options.text: David entered Saul's service purely for his musical talent, with no larger purpose in the narrative.
options.note: His music is the stated occasion, but the narrative places this within the larger story of God quietly establishing His anointed one.

options.text: David forced his way into Saul's service in order to seize power early.
options.note: David is sent for by Saul through a servant's recommendation; he does not force his way in.

options.text: David never actually entered Saul's service in this chapter.
options.note: Verses 21-23 explicitly describe David entering Saul's service and becoming his armor-bearer.

questions: Samuel almost anointed Eliab because of his impressive appearance. Where are you tempted to judge people, or even yourself, by outward appearance rather than the heart?
David was out tending sheep, overlooked even by his own family, at the very moment God had already chosen him. Where do you feel overlooked right now, and how might God be quietly at work in you?
The Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David the moment he was anointed, equipping him for a calling he would not step into for years. How is God preparing you today for something you cannot yet see?

Saul's spirit of distress is a sober reminder that turning from God can leave a person tormented even while still sitting on a throne. Is there an area where you have drifted from God and feel the resulting unrest?
David served faithfully in obscurity, as a musician and an armor bearer, long before he was crowned. What faithful, unseen service is God asking of you while you wait on what He has promised?

translationNotes.note: The LORD's words play on two Hebrew ideas: man judges by mar'eh, outward appearance, while the LORD examines the lebab, the heart, the inner seat of character and intention hidden from human sight.
The BSB footnote notes Shammah is a variant of Shimeah, Shimea, and Shimei found elsewhere for this brother, 2 Samuel 13:3, 2 Samuel 21:21, and 1 Chronicles 2:13.

The BSB footnote allows 'a spirit of distress' to be rendered 'a harmful spirit,' the same phrase recurring in verses 15, 16, and 23; the text affirms it comes from the LORD while showing it torments Saul rather than blessing him.
